clinicalPearls: Belongs to the oral-facial-digital group of ciliopathies that affect the mouth, face and digits
Oral findings include a lobulated or bifid tongue, midline notching of the upper lip and multiple hyperplastic oral frenula
Facial features are hypertelorism, a broad nasal bridge and a bifid nasal tip
Digital anomalies typically include polysyndactyly, with reduplication of the great toe (preaxial hallucal polydactyly) a helpful pointer
Conductive hearing loss from middle-ear ossicular anomalies is characteristic and helps distinguish it from some other subtypes
Inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, in contrast to the X-linked oral-facial-digital syndrome type I (OFD1)
Cognition is usually preserved, though brain malformation occurs in a minority
reference.pathophysiology: The oral-facial-digital syndromes are ciliopathies in which proteins localising to the basal body and primary cilium fail to support normal ciliary structure and signalling. In the midline structures of the developing face, the branchial arches and the limb buds, disrupted ciliary hedgehog signalling produces the clefting and lobulation of the tongue and lip, the hypertelorism and nasal anomalies, and the polysyndactyly with hallucal duplication that define the group. Type II (Mohr syndrome) follows autosomal recessive inheritance and is distinguished within the group by the combination of these oral and digital features with conductive hearing loss, separating it from the X-linked type I caused by variants in the ciliary gene OFD1.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed oral examination for tongue lobulation, frenula and midline clefting
Radiographs of the hands and feet to characterise polysyndactyly and hallucal duplication
Audiological assessment for conductive hearing loss
Brain imaging where central nervous system involvement is suspected
Molecular testing with an oral-facial-digital / ciliopathy gene panel
redFlags: Feeding or airway difficulty from oral and midline anomalies in infancy
Brain malformation with neurological or developmental consequences
Hearing loss threatening speech and language development
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have normal intellect and a good functional outcome with multidisciplinary craniofacial, dental and audiological care; prognosis is chiefly influenced by the presence and severity of any brain malformation.
pitfalls: Confusing autosomal recessive Mohr (type II) with the X-linked oral-facial-digital syndrome type I
Overlooking conductive hearing loss and its effect on language development
Missing preaxial hallucal duplication as a diagnostic clue
Assuming intellectual disability when cognition is usually normal
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Provide supportive, surgically-focused care with repair of oral anomalies (bifid or lobulated tongue, midline lip notching and hyperplastic frenula) and clefts
Correct digital anomalies including polysyndactyly and duplicated great toe
Manage conductive hearing loss with hearing aids, ventilation tubes or ossicular reconstruction
Coordinate dental and orthodontic care with craniofacial follow-up
Arrange brain imaging and developmental support where central nervous system involvement is suspected
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, distinguishing it from X-linked OFD type I
